pr_title: [3.x] Fix invalid string to numeric type cast yields 0.
pr_body:
This PR fixes a bug where casting a string variant to an integer results in 0. This bug is most noticable when passing a string as a parameter to a function that accepts an integer as a parameter such as `Array.remove`.

_Bugsquad edit: fixes #93113_
pr_comments: Here is the the exact issue this PR resolves: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/93113
The regex module can be disabled so you will need to check if it's enable and change the code depending on that
I have discovered that attempting to cast from a string to a float is also affected by the same bug, therefore I have expanded this fix to cover string to float conversion as well.

I resolved the regex issue by switching to a custom algorithm that isn't dependent on the `regex` module. This algorithm does more strict checking than the original one and correctly catches invalid characters at the beginning, middle, or end of the string as well as a negative sign with no numerals following it. It correctly allows literals that start with a decimal point as well.

Examples of invalid strings that are correctly identified:
```
"t1e2xt"
"-3a"
"3.14a"
"-3.14a"
```

Examples of valid strings that are correctly identified:
```
"3"
"3.14"
"-3.14"
"0.14"
".14"
```
I have confirmed that this bug is also present in Godot 4.3 https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/99601

This fix seems to be a reasonable addition to address the issue, but I think the real problem here is that `String` is convertible to `int` automatically in the first place. Operations that can fail like this should be explicit, such as `string.to_int()`, and automatic conversion should be disabled. I'm not sure if something like this is realistic to be mergable for a minor version upgrade, since it's a somewhat breaking change.

issue_context.title: Array.remove( int position ) accepts String as an argument instead of throwing error
issue_context.body:
### Tested versions

- Reproducible in: 3.5.3.stable, 3.5.stable, 3.3.4.stable

### System information

Apple M1 Pro 2021 running MacOS 14.1

### Issue description

In the [3.5 documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.5/classes/class_array.html#class-array-method-remove), it states that the remove() method for Array accepts one argument of the type int which indicates the position of element to be removed. However, the remove() method will accept a String without throwing an error, and removes the first element of the Array it's applied to, if a String is given.

See example code: 

```gdscript
	var arr = [0,1,2,3,4,5,6]
	arr.remove("text")
	print(arr) # Prints [1,2,3,4,5,6]
```

This code should throw an error, but it doesn't.

### Steps to reproduce

Run the code example above in a gdscript file

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

N/A
comments:
I can confirm that this bug is present on Windows 11 as well:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bbd33452-cc5b-45cd-b72f-73472bc4842d)

I have successfully isolated the bug. If you run a test like this, you will notice that casting a string variant to an integer yields the integer 0:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fec33c30-f94c-4675-b5eb-7da548122534)

It turns out that the culprit appears to be this block of code:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8ca617d7-8c1c-4ac6-9d50-474cad17e2e8)

When the signed int operator of the variant class is used to convert a string variant to a signed integer, it is returning 0. Which is then passed into the `Array.remove` method and resulting in the first element being removed.

I'll do further testing to find a possible solution to this bug.

**Update:** The reason why the value 0 is returned is caused by the structure of the `String::to_int` method here:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/caaa5b6b-ebcf-4895-8fe0-7e9ab9868c4e)

Since the `integer` variable is initialized to 0 and the loop skips over non-numeric characters other than "-", the string "test" has a value of 0 when `to_int` is called on it.

**Update:** The current algorithm in `to_int` also has odd behavior when the string contains a numeral in the middle of the string:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b111c956-3e19-417b-915e-88f735bc796a)
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9a0ddfbd-6d19-4e86-bdfa-9c369cdf8ffa)

**Update:** This bug is also present if you simply convert a string to an integer:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5d76fa7f-e455-4d48-bd81-de59bd26cf6c)

After doing further research, I have come to the following conclusions:
* once we have begun the conversion process, there is no reasonable way to bail out since the return value must be an integer and we cannot reserve a specific value as an error value
* what we really need to do, is determine if converting the string to an integer makes sense given its contents and bail out before performing the conversion
* since the `Variant::can_convert` method gets called before attempting to convert the string to an integer, it appears to be an ideal place to also check if it makes sense to convert the string to an integer
* however, `Variant:can_convert` is a static method and therefore has no access to the contents of the string we are attempting to convert
* we could add an extra parameter to `Variant::can_convert` that accepts the variant as a parameter in addition to the to and from types or we could make `Variant::can_convert` an instance method instead of static
* inside we would then be able to test if the to type is int and the from type is string, then check for invalid characters in the string and return false if we find any
* another possible solution that would be faster is to only check if the string starts with a numeral or a "-" followed by a numeral
* either way, we would have to refactor all lines that call `Variant::can_convert` which is a total of 15 lines across 7 files according to VS code

Does anyone have any thoughts on these observations?
I'll go ahead and prepare a patch to fix this bug and submit a PR soon.

Some parts of the code require the static method syntax and can't be refactored because there is no actual variant instance to call the instance method on (like when we are checking the type of nodes in visual scripts), so I will opt to instead simply add an instance version of `Variant::can_convert` to use whenever possible and keep the static version for situations where calling the instance method isn't possible.

review_comments: I think it's very confusing that `can_convert(Type p_type_to)` is not a non-static wrapper around `can_convert(Type p_type_from, Type p_type_to)`, but contains additional logic.

The additional logic in `can_convert(Type p_type_to)` requires an instance of `Variant` which wouldn't be available from the static version of the method. Notice that line 609 of `core/variant.cpp` must call `operator String()` in order to fetch the value of the string that is attempting to be converted. The only solution I can see would be refactoring all parts of the code that call the static version of the method so they instead call the instance version of the method and move all the logic to the instance method.

In my opinion, this approach is unacceptable. Please either choose a different name for the method, or make the behavior consistent for static and non-static versions, or replace `can_convert()` with in place checks or maybe even use `can_convert_strict()` (can be breaking).

Also, this requires research for compatibility with 3.6 and consistency with 4.x. If it has the same bug, then we should fix it in 4.x first. It is not desirable to have differences with 4.x in such methods without a good reason.

Making the behavior consistent would require adding a third parameter to the static version of `Variant::can_convert` which accepts an instance of a `Variant`. This wouldn't work since in cases where there is no instance and would require a change in the function signature. It also would defeat the purpose of having the instance version of the method.

In place checks would be messy because they would require the type to be checked in order to know if the conversion is from a string to a numeric type beforehand. Which in turn would require an additional if block in every part of the code where `Variant::can_convert` is called.

Using `can_convert_strict` instead wouldn't make much sense and would still require a change in the function signature.

So the only option left is renaming the function.

This bug will need to be checked for in 4.x and fixed there if present. Until that is handled and compatibility with 3.6 is researched, there is no path forward for fixing this bug.
You can use `String.is_valid_integer()` and `String.is_valid_float()` methods instead.
